title: sandbox-llm-serving-accelerator-workshop-notes
body:
Overview:
This hands-on workshop is a compact, repeatable POC to show customers how to run a small LLM serving stack in a constrained environment (single GPU or CPU-only fallback). The goal is to demonstrate observable latency/cost tradeoffs from: baseline FP16 GPU serving, ONNX quantized CPU serving, and a GPU fallback path. The lab uses a sandbox repo (linked above), Docker compose for local demos, and a lightweight k8s manifest for a minimal on-prem test cluster.

Audience and Goals:
- Audience: Solutions engineers + customer infra engineers.
- 90-minute timebox covering environment setup, three experiments, and a short troubleshooting/analysis section.
- Deliverables: working local endpoint, sample client script, simple dashboard metrics, and a short artifacts zip for customers to try later.

Prerequisites (participants should have):
- Laptop with Docker & docker-compose installed (or a small k8s cluster like kind/minikube).
- Optional: 1x NVIDIA GPU + nvidia-docker for the GPU part; if not available, the workshop will use CPU-only ONNX mode.
- Python 3.10+, pip, curl.
- GitHub access to the poc-llm-accelerator repo.

Timeplan (90 minutes):
- 0-10m: Intros + objectives + architecture diagram walkthrough.
- 10-30m: Local sandbox bring-up via docker-compose (baseline FP16 server if GPU present).
- 30-50m: Run quantized ONNX CPU variant, run client load, observe metrics.
- 50-70m: Enable routing policy to fallback from CPU to GPU variant (or vice versa), run regression/assertion tests.
- 70-85m: Troubleshooting common issues, inspection of logs and metrics.
- 85-90m: Wrap-up, next steps, customer follow-ups.

Architecture (compact):
- model-server: Redwood-compatible serving runtime replica(s) exposing inference HTTP API.
- router: simple policy container that routes requests to server variants (cpu-onnx, gpu-fp16).
- client: python test harness that runs functional + latency tests and pushes metrics to the dashboard.
- observability: Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint + Grafana snapshot (pre-built dashboard JSON in repo).

Quickstart (local, docker-compose)
1) Clone the repo:
   git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/poc-llm-accelerator.git && cd poc-llm-accelerator

2) Start sandbox (CPU-only fallback):
   # CPU-only flow (no GPU required)
   docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.cpu.yml up --build -d

3) Check services:
   docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.cpu.yml ps

4) Run the client smoke test:
   python client/smoke_test.py --endpoint http://localhost:8080/infer --model small-onnx-q4

Docker-compose snippet (cpu file)
version: '3.8'
services:
  model-server:
    image: redwood/poc-serve:latest
    command: ["--model", "small-onnx-q4", "--port", "8080"]
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      - SKIP_GPU=1
  router:
    image: redwood/poc-router:latest
    ports:
      - "8081:8081"
    depends_on:
      - model-server
  metrics:
    image: prom/prometheus:latest
    volumes:
      - ./monitoring/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro

Kubernetes manifest (minimal, use kind/minikube)
# deployment-onnx-cpu.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: llm-onnx-cpu
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: llm-onnx-cpu
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: llm-onnx-cpu
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: model-server
        image: redwood/poc-serve:latest
        args: ["--model", "small-onnx-q4", "--port", "8080"]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080

Sample Python client (client/smoke_test.py)
(put this into the repo as client/smoke_test.py)
"""
Simple load/generate client showing latency and correctness assertions"""
import time
import requests

ENDPOINT = "http://localhost:8080/infer"
PAYLOAD = {"input": "Write a 2-line summary of Redwood Inference."}

def run_once():
    start = time.time()
    r = requests.post(ENDPOINT, json=PAYLOAD, timeout=30)
    latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000
    print(f"status={r.status_code} latency_ms={latency:.1f}")
    print(r.json())

if __name__ == '__main__':
    for i in range(5):
        run_once()

Experiment plan and checkpoints:
- Baseline (GPU FP16): single model-server with FP16 weights. Expect median token latency X and throughput Y. Record Prometheus metrics: tokens_served_total, request_latency_ms.
- Quantized ONNX CPU (q4/q8): bring up CPU server image, run the same prompts, compare output length, latency, and two sample quality checks (exact phrase presence and token-level divergence sampling).
- Routing/Fallback: use router container to direct 90% traffic to cpu variant and 10% to gpu variant; then simulate gpu OOM and ensure router escalates to CPU-only path while maintaining SLO.

Observability and dashboards:
- Prometheus job scrapes each model-server instance on /metrics. We surface: request_count, request_failed_count, p50/p90/p99 latency, tokens_generated.
- Grafana prebuilt dashboard file: monitoring/grafana/llm_sandbox_dashboard.json (import into local Grafana for the workshop).

Troubleshooting checklist (most common issues):
- Server fails to start: check logs docker-compose logs model-server; common cause is missing model file (git lfs submodule in repo).
- High CPU latency on ONNX: confirm quantized model used, check thread count, and set OMP_NUM_THREADS=2 for predictable latency.
- GPU not detected: ensure nvidia-docker is installed and docker-compose.gpu.yml is used; verify nvidia-smi inside container.
- Router 502 errors: router fell back to a stub; check router logs and health endpoints of downstream servers.

Quality checks (quick assertions to run after each experiment):
- Functional check: client/smoke_test.py returns 200 and non-empty "text" field.
- Determinism check: seed the generation if the model supports it and compare tokens across runs.
- Unit-economics: capture tokens_generated / second and estimate cost delta between cpu-onnx and gpu-fp16 for a small request profile.

Safety and data considerations:
- The sandbox uses toy models and synthetic prompts. For customer POCs with real data, recommend enabling audit logs and KMS integration.

Next steps and follow-ups for customers:
- If customer wants to validate scale, run the k8s manifests on a 3-node cluster and use the provided load generator in client/load_test.py.
- Offer a SKU for a week-long on-prem pilot with Redwood Private: include dedicated capacity sizing, SLA targets, and a migration checklist.

Appendix: quick commands collection
# Stop everything
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.cpu.yml down

# Start GPU variant (if GPU present)
docker-compose -f docker/docker-compose.gpu.yml up --build -d

# Run load test
python client/load_test.py --endpoint http://localhost:8081/route --concurrency 8 --duration 60

Contact and ownership:
Author: Evelyn Park (solutions engineering)
Workshop kit repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/poc-llm-accelerator
Notes: Keep a log of any customer-specific model sizes and latency targets and attach as follow-up doc for dedicated sizing.
